1000484.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Ísland, from íss (“ice”) + land (“land, country”), literally “ice land”. The name probably refers to drift ice seen by early seafarers off the northern parts of the island.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Island, Danish Island, Swedish Island, Faroese Ísland and Icelandic Ísland (“Iceland”). English Iceland is a calque of the Old Norse name.

1001252.etyen:
Borrowed from German Hannes, a short form of Johannes (“John”), ultimately from Late Latin Iōhannēs, a variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”). In Norwegian, Hannes has also historically been used as an older form of Hans.
Doublet of Hans and Johannes.
Compare Danish Hannes, Swedish Hannes, German Hannes, Finnish Hannes, Icelandic Hannes and Faroese Hannes (“male given name”).

1005092.etyen:
Variant of Anine (“female given name”). Store norske leksikon describes Annine as a derivative of the female given names Anna and Anne.
The name therefore belongs to the Anna name family, ultimately from Late Latin Anna (“female given name”), from Koine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna, “Anna”), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannāh, “Hannah; grace, favour”).
Compare Danish Annine and Swedish Annine (“female given name”).
